content:
Is the environment linting framework being upstreamed to core?

I noticed a couple PRs to core that seem to be related to doing so (e.g. lean4#13431), and was wondering what the plans are (how much is being upstreamed, how much is intended to remain in batteries, etc.). I don't recall seeing any discussion about this. Have I missed the memo, or is it a surprise? :)

There was some discussion, but none in a fully public place yet. Thanks for the reminder to change that. Below is a lightly edited version of an earlier message:

Thanks to the hard work of the Lean community, Batteries and mathlib contain many bits and pieces that improve the Lean user experience dramatically. With an increasing population of Lean users that don't live inside or downstream of mathlib, I think it would be great if these extra conveniences were available to as many people as possible.

For the next few months, Wojciech Różowski will be working on linters and elaborator goodies in Lean core. A significant part of this will be replicating, or, where possible, upstreaming material from Batteries and mathlib, and I am writing to give advance notice and explain our plans so that we have time for discussion.

The usual upstreaming disclaimer: the aim is not to take away any kind of control from the community. For upstreamed material, the original author retains the ability to modify it in core. If you ever feel that we don't keep this promise by ignoring/neglecting PRs to upstreamed material, you should personally bug me about this.

Without further ado, here is what Wojciech will be looking at:

  • Wojciech will be working on implementing support for deprecating more things: this includes names of function arguments, any kind of syntax (which in particular includes the possibility of deprecating tactics), and modules. In particular, we are planning to add a deprecated_module command that will be essentially identical to (and replace) the one in mathlib.
  • We would like to deprecate a bunch of tactics/syntaxes that mathlib lints against, like refine', stream-of-consciousness obtain, and so on.
  • Wojciech will implement a system in core that will be similar to the environment linter framework in Batteries with some added conveniences. The goal here is to unify the two kinds of linters a bit more and allow for some more control about when and how linter warnings are shown, to allow for "low-priority" lints that are only shown when explicitly invoking lake clippy (similar to cargo clippy) or similar. It will be no problem to run the extended core linter framework alongside the framework in Batteries.
  • There is a list of linters from Batteries and mathlib that we are interested in making available to all Lean users out of the box because we think they are valuable also outside of a mathlib context. These fall into several categories: first are linters that guard against what I think are just bugs in core. For these, we are planning to just fix the bug. Second are linters that we think would be valuable for all users, and third are linters that we would be interested in shipping, but not enabling by default (to be enabled by projects like mathlib as desired). Here is the list:

First category: guarding against bugs in core?

If you see any reason why these lints should not turn into hard errors, please let me know!

  • impossibleInstance: Check for instances with arguments that cannot be filled in by instance synthesis.
  • nonClassInstance: Check if non-class types are marked as instances.
  • simpVarHead: Check that the head of simp LHS is not a variable (after whnfR). Such lemmas never fire. (Update: this turned into a linter that checks for certain very general discr tree patterns which can be disabled)
  • globalAttribute: Warn on attribute [...] name in where in is misleading because the attribute is global.
  • modulesForbiddenWindows: Verify no module names use Windows-forbidden filenames (CON, AUX, etc.).

Second category: linters that we think would be valuable for all users

These would be the first ones we would consider upstreaming.

  • defLemma: Check whether def and theorem are used correctly
  • checkUnivs: Check for bad max u v levels where neither u nor v appear alone
  • docString.empty: Check for empty doc-strings

Third category: linters that we would like to provide but disabled by default

We would be interested in upstreaming these as time permits.

  • unreachableTactic: Warn on tactics that are never executed
  • unnecessarySeqFocus: Warn when <;> is used where ; suffices
  • dupNamespace: Check for repeated consecutive namespaces
  • multiGoal: Warn when multiple active goals remain after a tactic not expected to handle multiple goals.
  • unusedTactic: Warn when a tactic does not change anything
  • unusedDecidableInType: Check for Decidable instances unused in the theorem statement

For these new sorts of environment linters, will there be a way to have them automatically run on your file like currently syntax linters do?
People are writing very nice environment linters and it would be great to have a way of automatically getting the feedback from these linters while writing the files.
Currently people without CI in their personal projects don't really profit from these linters.

Also, one footgun with simp_all is, that currently it is very easily possible to write simp lemmas with impossible assumptions (assumptions which will always contain metavariables not inferable from the goal). I presume this is not convered by the simpVarHead linter?
And then there is also this unrelated lean#11798 simp bug which would be very nice to at least lint against while it is not fixed.
(Sorry if this is not the place for suggestions additions to your list)

Moritz Roos said:

For these new sorts of environment linters, will there be a way to have them automatically run on your file like currently syntax linters do?
People are writing very nice environment linters and it would be great to have a way of automatically getting the feedback from these linters while writing the files.
Currently people without CI in their personal projects don't really profit from these linters.

This seems a bit awkward to make automatic, but maybe if environment linting is being upstreamed it also makes sense to have a default lintDriver in core so that lake lint works out of the box?

Chris Henson said:

have a default lintDriver in core so that lake lint works out of the box?

Yes, Wojciech is working on this as we speak and it will be part of Lean 4.31.

Let me also mention this pre-rfc by @Thomas Murrills in this context.

Currently it is very awkward and inefficient to get the name of a/all new declarations (which might be autogenerated in case of an instance) in a syntax linter.
I believe this alone already is reason enough that people simply tend to write environment linters where syntax linters would be more or just as appropriate. This is a terrible but understandable reason.

Is there anything we can do to make this situation better?

CI /manually-evoked linters make a lot of sense for more global checks such as finding instance diamonds, but for per-declaration checks it would (i think) pretty much always be better if the linter would already give the feedback after completing the command (except maybe in cases where this would be too annoying).

I have to say I'm surprised that, despite having an excellent package manager in lake, the FRO seems to believe that the only way of distributing features to a wide range of lean users is to absorb it into the core lean distribution, making it harder to contribute to them and blocks availability of any improvements on updating to an entire new language version

Right now our approach is that if we believe that a linter we're interested in has correctness issues (particularly false positives, but also false negatives) then either we fix them during upstreaming (this happened for the simpVarHead linter for example), or we don't upstream it. Because of this I don't expect a huge amount of churn once a linter has landed upstream. And from the list in the original message you can see that the linters we're looking at are mostly simple and limited in scope compared to the more ambitious and experimental linters that are also present in mathlib.

More generally, I don't really buy the argument. Having a great out-of-the-box experience without having to add additional libraries (whoever may be maintaining them) is exactly the point. Maintaining a separate library (with the maintenance cost that implies, in particular having always at least two supported branches for the latest rc and the latest nightly) specifically for linters, just to be able to receive updates for this non-critical component of the system slightly faster, seems a bit silly.

I had a batteries PR that tried putting environment linters on the module system. My understanding was that some environment linters (but not all), such as simpNF, should run in a module, to mimick the typical uses of simp in mathlib, and to improve performance. Will this be supported?

I have another suggestion for a linter. Mathlib is full of letI and haveI that should just be let or have, and the question often comes up what the difference is, and in most cases the answer is that the I version should not have been used, and that there is no reason to have it. So, could we have a linter that warns when haveI or letI is used in a proof? And arguably we could also warn against uses of haveI and letI in meta definitions.
(btw lake lint was just merged #rss > Recent Commits to lean4:master @ 💬)

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

arguably we could also warn against uses of haveI and letI in meta definitions.

(Minor point, but note that letI can change the IR, for example, if you use letI f (a : A) := ... where f is a function used in multiple places! So it could have a use in meta code.)
Oh interesting, do you think this comes up in practice, where this is the motivation for using letI over let?

I've done it exactly once ever, where my motivation was inlining a conditional forallTelescope combinator (in an earlier version of the overlapping instances linter, as it happens!), but even then I wasn't super confident it was the right call or whether it mainly just hurt readability by being odd.

I haven't seen it much in meta code, to be honest, but that's the only reason I could imagine...usually if typechecking is failing without it there's something else that's wrong!
(Though actually, I wonder if sometimes it's also necessary for winning battles against Qq.)
